(Jan 01, 2021). "[https://www.britannica.com/biography/Li-Ye Li Ye: Chinese mathematician]". ''[[Encyclopaedia Britannica]]''. Accessed 7 February 2021.</ref><ref name="IdRef">"[https://www.idref.fr/185608124 Li, Ye (1192-1279) 李, 冶 (1192-1279)]"
 IdRef: ''Identifiants et Référentials pour l'enseignement supérieur et la recherche'' (French). Accessed 19 February 2018.</ref> was a Chinese mathematician, politician, and writer who published and improved the [[tian yuan shu]] method for solving [[polynomial equation]]s of one variable.<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/><ref name="MacTutor">{{cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Li_Zhi.html|title=Li Zhi Biography|last1=O'Connor|first1=John J.|last2=Robertson|first2=Edmund F.|authorlink2=Edmund F. </ref><ref name="Ho book">{{cite book|last=Ho|first=Peng Yoke|title=Li, Qi and Shu: An Introduction to Science and Civilization in China|publisher=Courier Dover Publications|year=2000|edition=unabridged|pages=89–96|isbn=0-486-41445-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_P6C4JO4JCUC&pg=PA89}}</ref><ref name="Scientific Biography">{{cite encyclopedia

== Name ==
Li Ye was born Li Zhi, but later changed his name to Li Ye to [[Naming taboo|avoid confusion]] with the [[Emperor Gaozong of Tang|third Tang emperor]] who was also named Li Zhi, removing one stroke from his original name to change the character. His name is also sometimes written as Li Chih or Li Yeh. His literary name was Renqing ({{zh|c=仁卿|w=Jen-ch’ing}})  and his [[Art-name|appellation]] was Jingzhai ({{zh|c=敬斋|w=Ching-chai}}).<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/><ref name="IdRef"/>

== Life ==
Li Ye was born in [[Daxing District|Daxing]] (now Beijing). His father was a secretary to an officer in the [[Jurchen people|Jurchen]] army.  Li passed the [[Imperial examination|civil service examination]] in 1230 at the age of 38, and was administrative prefect of Jun prefecture in [[Henan]] province until the [[Mongol–Jin Dynasty War|Mongol invasion in 1233]]. He then lived in poverty in the mountainous [[Shanxi province]]. In 1248 he finished his most known work ''Ceyuan haijing'' ({{lang|zh|測圓海鏡}}, ''Sea mirror of circle measurements'').<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/><ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, p. 40.</ref> Li then returned to [[Hebei]].

In 1257, [[Kublai Khan]], grandson of [[Genghis Khan]], ordered Li to give advice on science. In 1259, Li completed ''Yigu yanduan'' ({{lang|zh|益古演段}}, ''New steps in computation''), also a mathematics text. After becoming [[Khan (title)|Khan]], Kublai twice offered Li government positions, but Li was too old and in ill health. In 1264, Li finally accepted a position at the [[Hanlin Academy]], writing official histories. However, he had a political fallout and resigned after a few months, again citing ill health.<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/> He spent his final years teaching at his home near Feng Lung mountain in Yuan, [[Hebei]]. Li told his son to burn all of his books except for ''Sea mirror of circle measurements''.<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/>

== Mathematics ==
===Ceyuan haijing===
{{main|Ceyuan haijing}}
[[File:圆城图式.jpg|thumb|300px|The master figure in ''Sea mirror of circle measurements'', that all the problems use. It shows a circular city wall, inscribed in a right triangle and a square.]]
[[Ceyuan haijing]] (''Sea mirror of circle measurements'') is a collection of 170 problems, all related to the same example of a circular city wall inscribed in a [[right triangle]] and a square.<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/><ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, pp. 44, 129.</ref> They often involve two people who walk on straight lines until they can see each other, meet or reach a tree in a certain spot. The purpose of book was to study intricate geometrical relations with algebra and provide solutions to equations.<ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, pp. 44-45.</ref>

Many of the problems are solved by polynomial equations, which are represented using a method called [[tian yuan shu]], "coefficient array method" or literally "method of the celestial unknown".<ref name="andrea breard encyclopaedia britannica january 2021"/><ref name="needham ling 1995 p45">Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, p. 45.</ref> The method was known before him in some form.  It is a positional system of [[rod numeral]]s to represent [[polynomial equation]]s.

For example, 2x<sup>2</sup> + 18x − 316 = 0 is represented as

[[File:Polynomial equation with rod numerals.png]] which is equal to [[File:Polynomial equation in tian yuan shu with arabic numerals.png]] in Arabic Numbers.

The {{lang|zh|元}} (''yuan'') denotes the unknown x, so the numerals on that line mean 18x. The line below is the constant term (-316) and the line above is the coefficient of the quadratic (x<sup>2</sup>) term. The system accommodates arbitrarily high exponents of the unknown by adding more lines on top and negative exponents by adding lines below the constant term. Decimals can also be represented. Later, the line order was reversed so that the first line is the lowest exponent.

Li does not explain how to solve equations in general, but shows it with the example problems. Most of the equations can be reduced to the second or sometimes third order. It is often assumed that he used methods similar to [[Ruffini's rule]] and [[Horner scheme]].

===Yigu yanduan===
{{main|Yigu yanduan}}
[[File:益古第八问.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Problem 8 in Yigu yanduan]]
[[Yigu yanduan]] (''New steps in computation'') is a work of more basic mathematics written soon after Li Ye completed Ceyuan haijing, and was probably written to help students who could not understand ''Sea mirror of circle measurements''. Yigu yanduan consists of three volumes dedicated to solving geometrical problems on two tracks, through [[Tian yuan shu]] and geometry. It also contained algebraic problems, but with slightly different notations.<ref name="needham ling 1995 p45"/>

===Astronomy and shape of the earth===<!-- Most of this section is not about Li Ye, but about the flat earth theory. -->

The ''huntian'' ({{lang|zh|渾天}}) theory of the [[celestial sphere]] stipulated that the earth was [[Flat Earth|flat and square]], while the heavens were spherical in shape, along with celestial bodies such as the sun and moon (described by 1st-century AD polymathic scientist and statesman [[Zhang Heng]] like a [[crossbow]] bullet and ball, respectively).<ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, pp. 216-218, 227.</ref> However, the idea of a flat earth was criticized by the Jin dynasty astronomer [[Yu Xi]] (fl. 307-345 AD), who suggested a rounded shape as an alternative.<ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, pp. 220, 498.</ref> In his ''Jingzhai gu zhin zhu'' ({{lang|zh|敬齋古今注}}),<ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, p. 498; footnote i.</ref> Li Ye echoed Yu's idea that the [[Spherical Earth|Earth was spherical]], similar in shape to the heavens but smaller in size, arguing that it could not be square since that would hinder the movement of the heavens and celestial bodies.<ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, p. 498.</ref> 

However, the idea of a spherical earth was not accepted in mainstream Chinese science and [[Chinese cartography|cartography]] until the 17th century during the late [[Ming dynasty|Ming]] and early [[Qing dynasty|Qing]] periods, with the advent of evidence of European [[circumnavigation]] of the globe.<ref>Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling. (1995) [1959]. ''Science and Civilization in China: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth'', vol. 3, reprint edition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-05801-5}}, pp. 498-499.</ref> The flat Earth theory in Chinese science was finally overturned in the 17th century. [[Jesuit China Missions|Jesuits in China]] also introduced the spherical Earth model advanced by [[Ancient Greek astronomy|ancient Greeks]] such as [[Philolaus]] and [[Eratosthenes]]<ref>Cullen, Christopher. (1993). "Appendix A: A Chinese Eratosthenes of the Flat Earth: a Study of a Fragment of Cosmology in Huainanzi", in Major, John. S. (ed), ''Heaven and Earth in Early Han Thought: Chapters Three, Four, and Five of the Huananzi''. Albany: State University of New York Press. {{ISBN|0-7914-1585-6}}, p. 269-270.</ref> and presented in [[world map]]s such as [[Matteo Ricci]]'s ''[[Kunyu Wanguo Quantu]]'' published in [[Ming dynasty|Ming-dynasty]] China in 1602.<ref name="Baran">{{cite news|url=http://minnesota.publicradio.org/display/web/2009/12/16/tulip-map/|title=Historic map coming to Minnesota |last=Baran|first=Madeleine |date=December 16, 2009|publisher=Minnesota Public Radio|accessdate=19 February 2018|location=St. Paul, Minn. }}</ref>
